sweep_summary: One works with stress in the title for Mbabaram: Kager 1995 'On foot templates and root templates' (Linguistics Library 12). It is hybrid open access (cc-by-nc); the publisher PDF was downloaded, text-extracted and pp. 131-132 rendered and read as page scan, logged). Sec. 4 is a secondary report of Dixon 1991 with a 332-root tabulation: heavy syllables always stressed; initial /a/ never stressed (second-syllable stress); C-initial disyllables lexically split; trisyllables mostly sigma-2, some final with initial secondary stress. It refines but does not contradict the catalog's weight-hedged coding on Dixon 1991:360, and being derivative of Dixon 1991 it does not supersede the deciding source. No paywalled or unread items remain from this search of works with stress in the title. Note from earlier check notes held by the project (not a works with stress in the title): Dixon 1991 vol. 4 is HathiTrust full view (mdp.39015021573046, seq 376 = p. 360) but page delivery is blocked from this GCP host.

new_statements.quote: Mbabaɽam stress is complex and lexically variable. Heavy syllables are always stressed (14a-b). An initial /a/ never bears main stress, which usually falls on the second syllable (14b-d). Disyllabic full-vowel roots are stressed on either the second syllable (14e-f), or the initial syllable (14 g-h). Most trisyllabic full-vowel roots are stressed on the second syllable (14i-j), some on the final syllable with an initial secondary stress (14k-l): (14) b abúu 'ground' d aráman 'woomera' e ɟibú 'no good' f miɟál 'lip' g búmba 'ashes' h láŋgil 'light' i ḏambáɽa 'nulla nulla' k gùriḏál 'eaglehawk' l gùludún 'dove'

new_statements.reading: Main stress is lexically variable and weight-conditioned: long-vowel (heavy) syllables always take it; word-initial /a/ is never stressed, so a-initial words are stressed on the second syllable; consonant-initial disyllables are split between initial and final stress with no rule; trisyllables are mostly second-syllable stressed, a minority final-stressed with initial secondary stress. Kager's root counts in (15) (152 final-stressed vs 12 initial-stressed LL roots, 93 of the 152 a-initial) quantify the pattern from Dixon's 332-root vocabulary. This is fully consistent with the catalog's 'weight-hedged' coding and adds trisyllabic and secondary-stress detail the snippet chain lacks.

new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the catalog record (Dixon 1991 p. 360, weight-hedged: initial /a/ never stressed so a-initial words take second-syllable stress; C-initial disyllables lexically split, e.g. búmba initial) and with the Kager 1995 statement held by the project: the 1966 article's accent-marked forms instantiate both halves (all RS words V2-stressed; TS búmba, bárŋan initial vs gurgáɽa, dayáɽi, migúlu second) and búmba 'ashes' is the very example the catalog quote cites for initial stress. It adds nothing on vowel length/weight or secondary stress and gives no explicit rule, so 'agrees' rather than 'refines'. The Tindale & Birdsell sentence is a quoted third-party phonetic observation, not Dixo…
new_statements.rule_in_words: This article states no stress rule of Dixon's own: it defers the phonology to the companion TPS paper 'Mbabaram phonology' and only (a) quotes Tindale & Birdsell's 1941 observation that in polysyllables principal stress is 'often' on the second syllable, (b) names a 'stress peculiarity' as one of the things that make Mbabaram phonetically odd for its area, together with monosyllables and vowel-initial words, and (c) prints its Mbabaram citations with an acute on the stressed vowel. Those marked forms show every a-initial (RS) word stressed on the second syllable (arí, amí, aŋál, aɽú, alŋú, abú, abí, abá; aramán on the final of three) and consonant-initial (TS) words split between initial stress (bárŋan 'kangaroo-rat', búmba 'ashes') and second-syllable stress (gurgáɽa, dayáɽi, migúlu; yaramán 'horse' final), i.e. placement is not fixed and must be given per word apart from the a-initial regularity: exactly the picture the catalog codes from Dixon 1991 (initial /a/ never stressed; C-initial disyllables unpredictable, búmba among the initial-stressed examples there too).
new_statements.secondary_stress: nothing said; only one accent per word is marked
new_statements.exceptions: none stated as such; Tindale's hedge 'often placed on the second syllable' and the initial-stressed TS forms bárŋan, búmba are the visible departures from second-syllable stress
new_statements.identity_note: Mbabaram (Tindale's 'Barbaram'), recorded by Dixon in 1963-64 with Albert Bennett as the Mbabaram informant (fn. 4), one of the few remaining speakers of a language 'not actively spoken' for years (p. 97); territory around Irvinebank, Petford and Lappa, north Queensland (p. 107 and map p. 109); the comparative sections cite Dyangun (Kuku Jangkun), Agwamin (Wagaman), Muluridyi and Dyirbal forms but describe only Mbabaram.
